clue.text: Freedom from restriction for adult wearing tie

indicators.note: something wearing is being worn down and knocked out of shape, so the letters lose their order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A grown-up in a tie claims some freedom from rules.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wearing' reads as a grown-up dressed in a tie, but here it means worn out of shape, so ADULT and TIE are rearranged together.
explanation.definitionFit: Latitude is scope or leeway to act as one chooses, which is exactly freedom from restriction.

clue.text: Urge politician to join international party

blocks.note: Lib is short for a Liberal politician
I is the abbreviation for international
a do is an informal word for a party

explanation.surface: Someone presses a politician to sign up to a party with international links.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Urge' looks like a verb telling the politician what to do, but it is a noun naming the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Libido is sexual desire or drive, a powerful instinctive urge.

clue.text: Big cats make love one time when being brought up

indicators.note: in a down clue, something brought up is lifted from bottom to top, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: to snog is British slang for kissing passionately
the Roman numeral for one
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A slightly racy account of big cats mating, one time when they were being raised.
explanation.walkthrough: Snog is British slang for a long passionate kiss. Join it with I and T, then read the whole string upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A tigon is the hybrid offspring of a male tiger and a lioness, so tigons are big cats.

clue.text: Mild anger requires a note

blocks.note: a temper is a fit of anger
taken as written
te is the seventh note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A paradox: mild anger needs only a note, as in a polite letter of complaint.
explanation.definitionFit: Temperate weather or behaviour is moderate, free from extremes, which is what mild means.

clue.text: Handicaps the girl's talents

blocks.note: Di is a girl's name, so Di's means belonging to the girl
talents are natural abilities

explanation.surface: A girl's talents are described as her handicaps, a backhanded remark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Handicaps' looks like a verb with 'the girl's talents' as its object, but it is a plural noun defining the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Handicaps and disabilities are both physical or mental conditions limiting a person's activity, so the words are near synonyms.

clue.text: I had a meal after work — it puts me to sleep

blocks.note: op is short for opus, a musical work
taken as written
to have a meal is to eat, and had a meal is ate

explanation.surface: After a working day a big dinner sends me off to sleep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' tells you the meal follows the work, so OP comes first. The definition is a description rather than a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: An opiate is a drug derived from opium, which dulls the senses and induces sleep.

clue.text: Criticise books coming up as entertainment

indicators.note: in a down clue, coming up means travelling from the bottom to the top, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: to pan a show is to criticise it harshly
OT is the Old Testament, a collection of books of the Bible

explanation.surface: A reviewer criticises books that are being turned into entertainment.
explanation.walkthrough: Only 'books' is reversed: OT becomes TO. Panto is pantomime, a British family stage show put on at Christmas.
explanation.definitionFit: Pantomime is a traditional British form of comic theatre, so it is a kind of entertainment.

clue.text: Impermeable to musical theme?

blocks.note: surface reading: sealed so that nothing can pass through
setter's reading: a musical theme is a tune, also called an air, so something sealed against an air is proof against a tune

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the pun: a tune is called an air, so a seal against air could be read as a seal against music.
explanation.definitionFit: Something sealed so no gas can get in or out is impermeable, and the tune sense of air makes the cryptic reading.

clue.text: First Lady rents out horses for three day competitors

indicators.note: out here means out of order or put out of place, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: Eve was the first woman in the Bible
taken as written

explanation.surface: A president's wife lets out horses to people competing in a three-day event.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First Lady' suggests a president's wife, but it means Eve, the first woman. Three-day eventing combines dressage, cross-country and show jumping.
explanation.definitionFit: Eventers are horses, or riders, trained for eventing, the three-day equestrian competition.

clue.text: Great article on obscure criminal

blocks.note: great means big
a is the indefinite article
to mist is to obscure, as fog does

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece on an obscure criminal is called great.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Obscure' reads as an adjective for the criminal, but it is a verb giving MIST.
explanation.definitionFit: A bigamist marries while already married, which is a crime, so a bigamist is a criminal.

clue.text: Will the European Union turn out to be dishonest?

indicators.note: out here signals letters thrown out of their order and rearranged

blocks.note: EU is the abbreviation for the European Union
taken as written

explanation.surface: A political question about whether the European Union will prove dishonest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn out' looks like a phrasal verb meaning prove, but 'turn' is fodder and 'out' the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Something untrue is false, and a dishonest statement is one that is false.

clue.text: Do without oil? Lord, what a mixture of alternatives!

indicators.note: a mixture is a jumble, so the letters that follow are mixed up

blocks.note: to forgo something is to do without it
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims to the Lord about the choices facing a world that must manage without oil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Do without oil' reads as one phrase, but it splits: 'Do without' gives FORGO and 'oil' joins 'Lord' as anagram fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase covers both outcomes, good and bad, so it names a pair of alternatives; the definition is loose.

clue.text: Dead relative left out, the fool

indicators.note: out means removed, so the named letter is taken away

blocks.note: D is the abbreviation for dead
an uncle is a relative
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A family will-reading: a dead relative left the fool out of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left out' sounds like being excluded from a will, but 'left' gives L, which is removed from the relative.
explanation.definitionFit: A dunce is a slow-witted or stupid person, so a fool.

clue.text: Scientist may boil over, then go back with a first

indicators.note: over here means turned over or upset, so the letters are rearranged
going back means travelling in the opposite direction, so the word is read backwards

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
a first is the 1st, written out as 1ST with I for 1

explanation.surface: A lab scientist's experiment may boil over before a retreat with a first-class result.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boil over' sounds like a pan bubbling across its rim, but 'over' rearranges BOIL. A first is 1st, with the digit read as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: A biologist studies living organisms, so is one kind of scientist.

clue.text: Caught Raphael with girl, a weird writer

indicators.note: weird means strange or odd, so the letters take on an odd new arrangement

blocks.note: C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Gossip: the painter Raphael caught with a girl, by an odd writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Raphael reads as the Renaissance painter, but his name is simply anagram fodder along with 'girl'.
explanation.definitionFit: A calligrapher practises decorative handwriting, so is literally a writer of an artistic kind.

clue.text: Unhealthy reactions from colleagues about some work

indicators.note: about means around, so one word goes round the other

blocks.note: allies are colleagues or associates
an erg is a small unit of work in physics

explanation.surface: Bad reactions in the office from co-workers about some piece of work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some work' sounds like a task, but it is the erg, the physics unit of work, placed inside ALLIES.
explanation.definitionFit: Allergies are the body's harmful immune responses to substances, so unhealthy reactions.

clue.text: Don't allow cabin to be constructed in the watch tower

indicators.note: something constructed is built up from parts, so these letters are assembled in a new order

blocks.note: to bar something is to prohibit it
taken as written

explanation.surface: A planning ruling: no cabin may be built inside the watch tower.
explanation.walkthrough: A barbican is an outer defence of a castle, and the Barbican is also a London arts centre.
explanation.definitionFit: A barbican is a fortified gate tower on a castle wall, used as a lookout, so a watch tower.

clue.text: Son gathered everyone in the Channel Islands to see an onion

indicators.note: to have gathered something is to hold it collected inside, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for son
CI is the abbreviation for the Channel Islands
everyone means all
on can mean in, as in being on a team

explanation.surface: A son rounds everybody up on Jersey or Guernsey to look at an onion.
explanation.walkthrough: The Channel Islands lie off Normandy and belong to the British Crown. ALL goes inside CI; the final ON loosely stands for 'in', which comes earlier in the clue than its place in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A scallion is a spring onion or shallot, a mild variety of onion.

clue.text: Want nice lord to bring order to old universe

indicators.note: bringing order means arranging things afresh, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone wishes for a kindly lord to tidy up a chaotic old cosmos.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Want' reads as a verb of wishing, but it is the start of the anagram fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient world is the civilisations of antiquity, a whole old world, loosely an old universe.

clue.text: Ill will shown by married woman

blocks.note: M is the abbreviation for married
Alice is a woman's name

explanation.surface: A wife shows resentment, a marital spat in miniature.
explanation.definitionFit: Malice is the desire to harm others, which is the same as ill will.

clue.text: Hinders development of showy performances

blocks.note: first meaning: a verb, to stunt growth
second meaning: a noun, daring feats done for display

explanation.surface: A critic complains that flashy acts hold back real growth.
explanation.definitionFit: To stunt is to check growth, and stunts are also spectacular feats, so one word fits both a verb and a plural noun.

clue.text: It's freezing with nothing underneath

blocks.note: first meaning: colder than the freezing point of water
second meaning: placed under nought, read literally as a position beneath zero

explanation.surface: A cold day with nothing worn under the clothes, a shivery picture.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests going without underwear; read literally, the phrase puts something beneath nothing, i.e. under nought.
explanation.definitionFit: Temperatures under nought degrees Celsius are freezing, and the phrase also literally describes lying beneath nought.

clue.text: It was different in the middle

indicators.note: different means changed, so the letters are given a changed order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone recalls that things were not the same halfway through.
explanation.definitionFit: The waist is the narrow part of the body between ribs and hips, colloquially the middle.

clue.text: Sunday lunch a sort of stew? Complain!

blocks.note: first meaning: the traditional British Sunday meal of ... meat
second meaning: to criticise someone harshly

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles that the Sunday lunch came out more like a stew.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sunday roast is a British family meal of roast meat and vegetables. 'A sort of stew' is a loose aside: like stewing, roasting cooks food, and one can stew or roast in the heat.
explanation.definitionFit: A roast is the classic British Sunday lunch, and to roast someone is to criticise them severely.

clue.text: King Charles is repeatedly in trouble

blocks.note: CR is Carolus Rex, Latin for King Charles
the word is written twice

explanation.surface: A news line about the King repeatedly getting into difficulties.
explanation.walkthrough: Royal initials use Latin: Carolus Rex gives CR, as on old coins and post boxes.
explanation.definitionFit: A crisis is a time of serious difficulty or danger, which is a state of trouble.

clue.text: Polite Scotsman is not in the armed forces

blocks.note: civil means courteous
Ian is a typical Scottish man's name

explanation.surface: A courteous Scot turns out never to have served in the military.
explanation.definitionFit: Civilian as an adjective describes people outside the military, so not serving in the armed forces.

clue.text: Number in film in New York

indicators.note: in tells us one part sits inside another

blocks.note: taken as written
E.T. is the Spielberg film about an extra-terrestrial
NY is the abbreviation for New York

explanation.surface: A song or act appearing in a film set in New York.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number' looks like a song in a musical; here it is the defining figure, a count.
explanation.definitionFit: Ninety is the cardinal number nine times ten, so it is a number.

clue.text: Confuses viral infections with rest having abnormal development

indicators.note: abnormal development means growing in an irregular way, so the letters come out disordered

blocks.note: flus are bouts of influenza, a viral infection
taken as written

explanation.surface: A doctor is baffled by viruses that resist bed rest and develop strangely.
explanation.definitionFit: To fluster someone is to make them agitated and muddled, which is to confuse them.
